title: Vikram's Spy Thriller Was Shot in Seven Countries Over Nine Years. A Courtroom Is Now Deciding If Anyone Gets to See It.
excerpt: Dhruva Natchathiram's legal saga reached the Madras High Court on Tuesday. The judges have reserved their order. The diaspora is watching.
body:
The most delayed film in Indian cinema history has found a new obstacle, and this time it isn't the pandemic, budget overruns, or creative differences. It is a courtroom.

**Dhruva Natchathiram**, the spy action thriller starring Vikram and directed by Gautham Vasudev Menon, was heard before a two-judge bench of the Madras High Court on Tuesday, June 2. Justices V Lakshminarayanan and GR Swaminathan listened to arguments from both sides — the director seeking permission to release his film, and investors seeking to block it — and reserved their order. In layman's terms: the film is in legal limbo. No release can happen until the judges announce their decision.

## A Film That Has Outlived Eras

To understand why Dhruva Natchathiram matters, you need to understand the sheer scale of its journey. The project was first announced in 2013 with Suriya in the lead. Gautham Menon shelved it after creative differences. He revived it in 2015 with Vikram, and production began in 2017. The film was shot across seven countries over the next several years, interrupted by financial difficulties and the COVID-19 pandemic. Principal photography finally wrapped in February 2023.

The film sat completed but unreleased for three more years. Menon's financial troubles — debts to investors who had funded the production — created a legal web that kept it locked away. In April 2026, Justice Senthilkumar Ramamoorthy passed a single-bench order permitting the release "on or before June 15," giving Menon a window to settle his debts from the film's earnings.

Menon responded with visible relief on social media: "Some men tried to destroy my career and stop my film from releasing, a film that's also the work of more than a hundred people. Another man, my legal counsel, assured me there's a way ahead."

Then the investors appealed.

## The Legal Tangle

On May 21, investors K Premkumar and K Punniyamoorthy filed appeals against the single-bench order at the Madras High Court. Menon, through his lawyer, informed the court of an attempt to release the film on June 18 — earning more time to sort out his financial obligations. The appeal was scheduled for hearing on June 2.

Tuesday's hearing saw both sides present their arguments. The judges' decision to reserve orders means a ruling is expected soon, but the timing is uncertain. Until that announcement, the film cannot be exhibited in theatres. The legal question isn't about the film's quality — which even its detractors haven't questioned — but about whether Menon has the right to profit from a production that was partially funded by investors he hasn't fully repaid.

## Why the Diaspora Cares

Dhruva Natchathiram has developed a near-mythological status among Tamil cinema fans worldwide. The trailer, released years ago, showcased a spy thriller of genuine international ambition — covert operatives moving through global cities, action sequences across continents, a sensibility closer to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy than typical Indian action fare. Vikram, who has built a career on transformative performances, reportedly delivered one of his most nuanced roles as a New York-based undercover agent leading an elite team called "The Basement."

For NRI audiences, the film represents something specific: Indian cinema reaching for a global visual language without abandoning its roots. Gautham Menon, who directed the beloved Vinnaithaandi Varuvaayaa and the Joshua franchise, has always been one of Tamil cinema's most cosmopolitan voices. His financial troubles have overshadowed his artistic ambitions, but the completed film sitting in a vault is a reminder of what Indian cinema could be when it thinks beyond domestic formulas.

The ensemble cast includes Ritu Varma, R. Parthiban, Radhika Sarathkumar, Simran, and Vinayakan. Music is by Harris Jayaraj. The film is subtitled "Chapter One — Yuddha Kaandam" (War Chapter), suggesting a multi-part spy saga that may never get its sequel if the first instalment cannot clear legal hurdles.

## What Happens Next

The Madras High Court's reserved order could go either way. If the judges uphold the single-bench order, the film could release within weeks — potentially in June or July 2026. If they side with the investors, Menon will need to find alternative means to settle his debts before any release is possible.

For a film that has already survived nine years of production limbo, the courtroom chapter feels cruelly appropriate. Dhruva Natchathiram was always about a mission against impossible odds. Its creator is now living the plot.
author: Diaspora Desk
